chapters.title: Chapter 6: Taxes on Getting Money Out of the Company

lessons.title: ESOPs and Employee Benefits: The Tax Angle for Employer and Employee

body.text: An ESOP is taxed twice, at two different moments, under two different heads. The first tax arrives when the employee exercises and has received no cash at all. Companies that do not explain this in advance end up with angry employees holding a tax bill for money they cannot yet touch.

children.text: This lesson is written for the people who design compensation as much as for those who account for it. If you sit in HR, learning and development, or founding a company, the decisions here reach every employee you hire.

body.title: The four moments in an ESOP, and which ones are taxed

events.title: The option is given
events.description: No tax. The employee has a right to buy shares later at a fixed exercise price, and owns nothing yet.

events.title: The right becomes exercisable
events.description: Still no tax. Vesting only means the employee has served long enough to be allowed to exercise.

events.title: First tax point, as salary
events.description: The difference between fair market value on the exercise date and the exercise price is a perquisite, taxed at slab rates, with the employer deducting TDS under section 392 [old 192].

events.title: Second tax point, as capital gains
events.description: Sale price minus the fair market value already taxed at exercise. The holding period runs from the exercise or allotment date, not from grant.

body.latex: \text{Perquisite at exercise} = (\text{FMV on exercise date} - \text{Exercise price}) \times \text{Number of shares}
body.caption: For unlisted shares, fair market value comes from a merchant banker valuation

children.text: An engineer at an unlisted Bengaluru company holds 10,000 vested options with an exercise price of ₹10. She exercises when the valuation report puts fair market value at ₹300 a share. Three years later the company is acquired and she sells at ₹800.

cells: Tax at exercise, in the 30% bracket
Deducted by the employer from her salary
Her own money, out of pocket
Long-term capital gain on unlisted shares

body.text: Read rows two and three together. On exercise day she pays ₹1,00,000 to buy the shares and ₹9,04,800 in tax, a cash outflow of over ₹10 lakh, and receives nothing she can sell. In an unlisted company with no secondary market, that money is locked up for years. This is the single biggest reason employees let valuable options lapse.

stats.label: Cash out at exercise
stats.context: Exercise price plus perquisite tax, with no shares sold

stats.label: Tax at exercise
stats.context: Slab rate plus cess, on the full discount, as salary

stats.label: Tax on later gain
stats.context: 12.5% plus cess on long-term gains from unlisted shares

body.text: Notice the rate gap. The discount at exercise bears salary rates of up to 31.2%, while everything the share gains afterwards bears 13%. So the earlier an employee exercises, at a lower valuation, the more of the eventual upside falls into the cheaper bucket. That is the whole logic behind early exercise, and it trades tax efficiency against the risk of paying for shares that may never be worth anything.

body.title: The startup deferral, for companies that qualify

children.text: The law recognises the cash trap, but the relief is narrow. It is available only to startups that hold DPIIT recognition and a certificate from the Inter-Ministerial Board under section 140 [old 80-IAC], which is a much smaller group than the set of companies that call themselves startups.

For those employers, the perquisite tax at exercise can be deferred to the earliest of three triggers: 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year, the date the employee sells the shares, or the date the employee leaves the company. The deferral changes the timing, not the amount, and the trigger that catches people is the third one, because employees who resign lose the deferral immediately even if the shares remain unsellable.

body.title: Try It: The Perquisite at Exercise
body.prompt: An employee exercises 4,000 options at an exercise price of ₹25, when the valuation report puts fair market value at ₹340 a share. What is the perquisite taxable as salary? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: 4,000 × (₹340 minus ₹25) is ₹12,60,000, or ₹12.6 lakh. In the 30% bracket that is about ₹3,93,120 of tax with cess, due in the month of exercise, plus the ₹1,00,000 she pays to buy the shares. If she later sells at ₹600, her capital gain is 4,000 × (₹600 minus ₹340), or ₹10,40,000, because the ₹340 has already been taxed once.

body.title: Quick Check: What Is the Cost for Capital Gains?
body.question: An employee exercised at a fair market value of ₹300 when the exercise price was ₹10, and later sells at ₹800. What figure is used as the cost when computing her capital gain?
options: ₹300, the value already taxed as a perquisite
Nil, since the shares were granted free
body.explanation: ₹300. The gap between ₹10 and ₹300 has already been taxed as salary, so taxing it again as capital gain would be double taxation. The capital gain is therefore ₹500 a share. Using ₹10 as the cost is a common filing error that overstates the gain by the amount already taxed at exercise.

children.text: What the Employer Has to Do

body.title: The same ESOP, from two sides

columns.label: The employee's position
points: Nothing taxed at grant or vesting
Perquisite taxed as salary at exercise, at slab rates
Capital gains at sale, measured from the exercise value
Holding period runs from exercise, not from grant

columns.label: The company's position
points: Must obtain a valuation to fix fair market value at exercise
Must deduct TDS on the perquisite in the month of exercise and deposit it
Reports the perquisite in the employee's salary records and certificate
The ESOP cost charged in the accounts has been held allowable as employee compensation, though this rests on case law rather than an express provision

body.text: TDS on a perquisite is deducted from cash salary, because the perquisite itself is not cash. An employee exercising a large grant can therefore see an entire month's take-home pay disappear. Tell people this before exercise windows open, not in the payslip.

Tax-free up to ₹7,50,000 a year in total across all three, with the excess and the returns on it taxed as a perquisite
Deductible, subject to the usual payment timing rules
Employer NPS contribution within the limit
Deductible for the employee up to 14% of basic salary and dearness allowance, and this survives inside the default personal regime
Company car available for personal use
Taxable perquisite, valued under prescribed rules
Deductible only to the extent it is a business expense
Taxable perquisite, valued under prescribed rules
Reimbursement of actual business expenses on production of bills
Not a perquisite, because it is not income

body.label: The retirement contribution ceiling
body.context: Employer contributions to provident fund, NPS and superannuation are tax-free for the employee only up to this combined figure. It starts to bite at around ₹29 lakh of annual basic pay, so it affects senior hires rather than most of the team.

body.text: Salary structuring has become a much smaller lever than it was. Under the default personal regime in section 202 [old 115BAC], most of the old exemptions such as house rent allowance and leave travel allowance do not apply, leaving the ₹75,000 standard deduction and the employer NPS contribution as the two that still work. Benefits packages built around allowance engineering are usually designing for a regime most employees are no longer in.

body.title: Scenario: The Resignation That Triggered a Tax Bill
body.scenario: A DPIIT-recognised startup with a valid Inter-Ministerial Board certificate granted ESOPs to its first fifteen employees. Several exercised last year and used the startup deferral, so no tax was paid at exercise. Two of them have now resigned to join a larger company. The startup's shares are unlisted, there is no buyback offer and no secondary sale in sight.
body.prompt: What happens to those two employees, and what should the company do?
body.modelAnswer: Leaving the company is one of the three triggers that ends the deferral, alongside 48 months from the end of the relevant assessment year and an actual sale of the shares. So the perquisite tax both employees deferred now becomes payable, even though they still cannot sell a single share. The amount was fixed at exercise, based on fair market value then, and does not change because the company's value has since moved. Three things follow. The company must handle the TDS and reporting correctly on exit, and should tell both employees the exact amount and timing in writing rather than letting them discover it when filing. The employees need to plan cash, and should ask whether the company will facilitate a partial buyback or a secondary sale, which is the only real source of liquidity available to them. For everyone still employed, the company should explain plainly at the next exercise window that the deferral ends on resignation, because an employee who understands that may prefer to time exercise around a liquidity event instead. The broader design lesson for founders and HR teams is that the deferral solves timing only where the employee stays, and a company that grants ESOPs without any plan for liquidity has given its team an asset that generates tax bills before it generates money.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Combined Ceiling
body.textWithBlank: Employer contributions to provident fund, NPS and superannuation are tax-free for an employee only up to a combined ₹___ lakh a year.
body.explanation: ₹7.5 lakh across all three schemes taken together. Anything above it is taxed as a perquisite in the employee's hands, and so are the returns earned on the excess, which is the part people forget when they see only the contribution figure on a payslip.

body.title: Running an ESOP Scheme Without Surprises
steps: Get a fresh valuation before each exercise window, and keep the report on file
Compute the perquisite per employee and tell them the tax amount before they decide to exercise
Deduct TDS in the month of exercise and deposit it by the 7th of the next month
Check whether you actually hold DPIIT recognition and the Inter-Ministerial Board certificate before promising any deferral
Explain the three deferral triggers in the grant letter, especially the one that fires on resignation
Track exercise dates per employee, since holding periods for capital gains run from there
Plan a liquidity route, such as a periodic buyback or secondary sale window, before granting widely
Review the benefits package against the default personal regime, rather than against exemptions most employees can no longer claim

cards.definition: The four stages of an ESOP. Only exercise and sale are taxed.
A non-cash benefit from employment, taxed as salary. For ESOPs it is the discount at exercise.
The fixed price at which the employee can buy the shares, set at grant.
The valuation used to compute the perquisite, and the cost base for the later capital gain.
A timing relief for eligible startups, postponing perquisite tax to the earliest of 48 months, sale, or leaving employment.
The startup tax provision whose certificate is a condition for offering the ESOP deferral.
TDS on salary, including on the ESOP perquisite, deducted in the month of exercise.

points: ESOPs are taxed at exercise as a salary perquisite and again at sale as capital gains
The perquisite is fair market value at exercise less the exercise price, taxed at slab rates of up to 31.2%
The capital gain is measured from the exercise value, so the amount already taxed is not taxed twice
Exercise creates a cash outflow with no cash inflow, which is the central problem with ESOPs in unlisted companies
Eligible DPIIT-recognised startups can defer the perquisite tax to the earliest of 48 months, sale, or the employee leaving
Employer contributions to provident fund, NPS and superannuation are tax-free only up to ₹7.5 lakh combined
Employer NPS contributions up to 14% of basic pay remain deductible inside the default personal regime, unlike most old allowances
Companies that grant ESOPs owe their teams a plain explanation of the tax and a plan for liquidity

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Perquisite valuation rules, contribution limits and startup eligibility conditions are prescribed by rules and change. Confirm the current position with a qualified chartered accountant before designing or exercising an ESOP scheme.
